papers.title: Resonant Recognition Model analysis of cGAS: conserved spectral frequencies and a divergent naked mole-rat phase signature
papers.abstract: Background: Cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS) is a cytosolic DNA sensor with additional noncanonical nuclear functions, including suppression of homologous recombination (HR) in humans. In the naked mole-rat (NMR), cGAS instead promotes HR through a FANCI-RAD50-dependent mechanism, a functional reversal attributed to four C-terminal amino acid substitutions. Whether such functional divergence is reflected in primary-sequence-derived spectral features is unknown. Methods: We applied the Resonant Recognition Model (RRM) to cGAS sequences from fourteen mammals and to FANCI sequences from eight species. Sequences were converted to numerical series using EIIP values and analyzed by discrete Fourier transform; consensus spectra were generated by point-wise multiplication of individual power spectra. Phase differences between cGAS and FANCI were computed at frequencies of interest. Spectral amplitudes at the dominant shared frequency were correlated with body mass, lifespan, and lifespan-to-body-mass ratio. RRM frequencies were converted to electromagnetic wavelengths using the Cosic formulation ({lambda} = 201/f_RRM). Results: The cGAS consensus spectrum contained four prominent peaks (f = 0.0392, 0.0765, 0.2539, 0.4229), with 0.2539 dominant. Three FANCI peaks (0.04138, 0.2479, 0.4332) were close to cGAS peaks, and the combined cGAS+FANCI consensus retained peaks at 0.2539 and 0.04077. Spectral amplitude at f = 0.2539 correlated with body mass (r = 0.647, p < 0.05) and with lifespan-to-body-mass ratio (r = -0.677, p < 0.01); the NMR showed the lowest amplitude. Human cGAS-FANCI phase difference was 3.1297 rad, 0.0118 rad from opposition, satisfying the RRM interaction criterion; the NMR cGAS-FANCI pair gave 1.7319 rad, approximately {pi}/2, which does not satisfy the criterion. Conversion of the dominant frequency yielded a predicted wavelength of 792 nm (378.5 THz), in the near-infrared range. This prediction is testable in transparent vertebrate models: zebrafish respond to NIR light, and red-light pre-treatment has been reported to improve survival after lethal gamma irradiation in zebrafish embryos. Conclusions: RRM identifies conserved spectral features in cGAS consistent with a cGAS-FANCI relationship, and amplitude at the dominant frequency varies with life-history traits. The phase analysis does not support a direct interaction signature for NMR cGAS-FANCI, a negative result consistent with a chromatin-mediated mechanism. The cross-species phase comparisons suggest that NMR FANCI, not only NMR cGAS, may contribute to the distinctive interaction mode. The predicted 792 nm wavelength provides a concrete, experimentally accessible parameter for testing whether RRM-derived frequencies can modulate radiation resistance in a transparent vertebrate model. These results are hypothesis-generating and require experimental validation.

papers.title: Genome-wide loss of chromatin accessibility coexists with selectively elevated RNA abundance in nutrient-starved U2OS cells
papers.abstract: Background Chromatin accessibility is widely used as a proxy for regulatory potential and is often interpreted together with RNA-seq to infer gene-regulatory responses. However, the quantitative relationship between chromatin accessibility and transcript abundance may become difficult to interpret, particularly under acute cellular stress. Metabolic challenges such as nutrient deprivation are known to induce extensive chromatin remodelling and transcriptional reprogramming, raising the question of whether changes in transcript abundance are directly governed by chromatin accessibility in these contexts. Clarifying this relationship is critical for interpreting epigenomic data under stress conditions, and requires careful distinction between Tn5 accessibility, relative steady-state RNA abundance and transcriptional output. Results We integrated ATAC-seq and RNA-seq analyses in human U2OS osteosarcoma cells following 18 h of severe nutrient deprivation. We found that starvation was associated with a genome-wide reduction in accessibility and almost all significantly altered accessible regions showed reduced signal relative to actively growing cells. This decrease affected promoter- and enhancer-associated regions alike, including housekeeping-gene promoters and CTCF-motif sites. In contrast, RNA-seq revealed a more selective change in relative steady-state RNA abundance: only a minority of expressed genes were differentially regulated, and approximately 64% of differentially expressed genes showed increased relative RNA abundance. Changes in accessibility and transcript abundance were modestly correlated at promoters (Pearson r = 0.25) and weakly at enhancers (r = 0.10), and together explained only ~6% of the variance in transcript abundance changes. The relationship was graded: genes with the smallest promoter losses were about four times as likely to show increased RNA abundance as genes with the largest losses, independently of baseline promoter accessibility. Within-condition analyses similarly showed only modest relationships between promoter accessibility and RNA abundance in both actively growing and starved cells. Pathway-level analysis of mRNA abundance revealed the expected repression of biosynthetic and growth-related programmes, including ribosome biogenesis, translation and cellular growth, together with a less anticipated relative activation of stress-adaptive programmes, including extracellular matrix organisation, lipid and cholesterol metabolism, small GTPase signalling and developmental processes. For genes within these activated programmes, increased steady-state mRNA abundance was observed despite reduced ATAC-seq accessibility at associated regulatory regions. Exon-intron analyses of RNA-seq data indicated that these changes predominantly reflect altered RNA production. Metabolic labelling of nascent RNA at selected loci confirmed increased transcription of genes involved in adaptive programmes despite reduced promoter and enhancer accessibility, alongside with reduced production of biosynthetic transcripts and rRNA. Conclusions These findings demonstrate that chromatin accessibility and steady-state RNA abundance are only modestly coupled during severe nutrient deprivation, against a baseline of similarly modest promoter accessibility-abundance coupling. This underscores the limited ability of ATAC-seq accessibility to predict transcript abundance under this stress condition and supports a model in which chromatin accessibility acts as a permissive rather than deterministic layer of gene regulation. The selective induction of adaptive programmes, confirmed here at the level of RNA production, shows that transcriptional activation can occur despite genome-wide loss of ATAC-seq accessibility. Because ATAC-seq reports Tn5 accessibility rather than physical chromatin compaction, we interpret compaction as a plausible mechanistic model compatible with the current observations, which will require direct orthogonal validation.

papers.title: TileScope quantifies spatial gene expression relationships beyond colocalization
papers.abstract: Gene expression patterns within the same tissue region can exhibit similar correlation or enrichment, but still differ in their organization within regions and at their boundaries. We present TileScope, a framework for analysing genes and transcriptional programs within predefined tissue regions, their components and their contacts with neighbouring regions. TileScope combines regional enrichment, within-region correlation, cross-correlation over distance and expression differences near specific boundaries. Repeated spatial partitions and consensus aggregation show how these measurements depend on the grouping of spots or cells. Across 30 controlled constructions derived from glioblastoma and hepatocellular carcinoma data representing ten spatial expression scenarios, combined measurements separated arrangements that individual statistics left ambiguous, including coincident patches, gradients and expression localised at region boundaries. In 30 human glioblastoma sections, TileScope distinguished shared regional enrichment from internal covariation and identified hypoxia-associated expression localised at region boundary despite negligible within-region correlation. In newly acquired Visium profiles of control and myeloid-targeted MCT1-knockout (KO) orthotopic GL261 mouse gliomas, proliferation and myeloid programs were enriched in tumour peripheries but showed opposite within-periphery-region correlations. Proliferation was higher near the tumour-facing boundary in both samples, whereas myeloid expression was higher near the tumour-facing boundary in the control and farther within periphery in the KO condition. Xenium applications on glioblastoma and breast cancer samples demonstrated feasibility with irregularly spaced individual cells and different regional annotations. TileScope provides spatially explicit descriptions of gene and program relationships, linking their organization within tissue compartments to their sensitivity to aggregation.

papers.title: Development and cross-cohort evaluation of a multimodal deep-learning model for ER, PR and HER2 status classification in breast cancer
papers.abstract: Background. Estrogen receptor (ER), progesterone receptor (PR) and HER2 status guide systemic treatment in breast cancer. Multimodal models are rarely benchmarked against key biomarker molecular baselines or evaluated for cross-cohort calibration. We assessed incremental value, dependence on label-proximal HER2 transcripts, and transport of discrimination and calibration. Methods. A model combining whole-slide images, transcriptomes, age and stage was developed in TCGA-BRCA (1051 patients; ER/PR/HER2 analysis sets: 1001/998/1006) and evaluated in CPTAC-BRCA (120 patients; 118/113/95). CPTAC had been observed during earlier development and included 13 HER2-positive cases. Analyses included paired model comparisons, transcript removal, alternative loss functions and recalibration. Internal discrimination used pooled out-of-fold predictions; external discrimination used fold-mean estimates, with ensemble calibration reported separately. Internal calibration and macro-AUC uncertainty were interpreted as exploratory. Results. Internal AUCs were 0.943 for ER, 0.901 for PR, and 0.860 for HER2; external AUCs were 0.952, 0.937, and 0.918, respectively. External macro-AUC was 0.936 for the multimodal model and 0.957 for logistic regression using ESR1, PGR, and ERBB2 (difference -0.021). Removal of the extended 29-transcript 17q12-q21 region changed HER2 AUC by -0.035 [-0.058 to -0.013] (95% CI) internally and by -0.042 [-0.089 to -0.007] externally relative to the baseline multimodal model. For external 15-model ensemble predictions, recalibrated HER2 expected calibration error (ECE) was 0.236, exceeding the ECE reference ceiling of 0.125, while calibration-in-the-large was -1.657 [-2.373 to -1.023] (profile-likelihood 95% CI), indicating systematic overprediction. ER and PR also showed overprediction. In paired fold-mean comparisons, HER2 ECE and Brier score favoured the three-transcript model (ESR1, PGR, and ERBB2). Conclusions. A multimodal deep-learning model achieved high discrimination across cohorts but did not demonstrate clear incremental value over a parsimonious three-transcript baseline, while cross-cohort calibration remained a substantial challenge. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating incremental value, calibration, and clinical utility alongside discrimination when assessing AI-based prediction models for medical use.

papers.title: DoAggregate: a pipeline for aggregation testing for rare-variant on a gene and pathway level
papers.abstract: Motivation Aggregation tests overcome the classical limitation of rare variant analysis in cohort study design. Choosing the right statistical test remains one of the biggest challenges. Existing tools fall short in offering a comprehensive solution that includes automatic data processing, testing across all genes, as well as exploration of broader genetic regions such as pathways and Gene Ontology (GO) terms. Most aggregation tests only report p-values and basic statistics, lacking in the presentation of cohort level statistics and comparison of results across whole genome or exome scales. Results We introduce DoAggregate, an innovative, scalable pipeline designed to address these challenges. DoAggregate enables users to perform aggregation tests across genes, pathways, and GO terms. It leverages Excalibur, an ensemble approach combining 36 distinct aggregation methods. The pipeline enhances data analysis by presenting over-representation analysis and aggregation results in detailed Excel sheets, complete with annotations and plots to facilitate nuanced interpretation and comparison. Applied to public exome data from the 1000 Genomes Project, DoAggregate tested 10,447 genes, 49 over-represented pathways and 36 over-represented GO terms in a single run, returning annotated, cohort-level results for each region. Availability and implementation DoAggregate source code, documentation and installation instructions as well as test data sets and results are freely available at https://github.com/boutrys/DoAggregate and released under the MIT license. The repository contains the serial implementation (R package), the parallel implementation for Slurm-based computer clusters and the web application.

papers.title: Integrated transcriptomic and epigenomic profiling of human cartilage reveals coordinated changes in fibronectin expression, splicing, and receptor signaling during osteoarthritis progression
papers.abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is defined by progressive loss of articular cartilage, but how chondrocytes change as the disease advances is unclear because most studies have focused on end-stage tissue. We profiled human knee articular cartilage across the full range of macroscopic OA grade, from young healthy to aged severe OA donors, by bulk RNA sequencing of 92 knees, single-nucleus RNA sequencing of 108,600 chondrocyte nuclei from 30 donors and single-nucleus multiome sequencing of 24 of these donors, treating grade as a continuous variable. With increasing grade, cartilage increased extracellular matrix (ECM) synthesis and remodeling genes, lost glucocorticoid-responsive, lipid-metabolic and antioxidant programs, and changed the splicing of a small set of ECM transcripts, led by the extra domain B (EDB) exon of fibronectin (FN1). Nine chondrocyte clusters were present in every disease stage and formed a continuum ordered by cartilage zone and hypertrophic differentiation, with PRG4+ superficial and COL10A1+ hypertrophic chondrocytes as the only distinct cell types at its ends and a pre-hypertrophic state between them. With grade, all clusters shared a response in which ECM production rose and homeostatic programs fell, and they differed in which of its components was strongest: ECM production in the superficial cells, the secretory pathway in the hypertrophic and CYTL1+ cells, and inflammatory signaling in the ANXA1+ and CRISPLD2+ cells. Inferred communication between chondrocytes was remodeled with stage. FN1 was induced in every cluster in excess of its fibril-assembly machinery, together with the fibronectin-cleaving protease HTRA1, and FN1 signaling shifted in receptor use from integrin 5{beta}1 toward CD44 and, less robustly, v{beta}8, accompanied by a rise in TGF-{beta}/SMAD response genes. In four early-OA donors, tenascin-C was already largely induced and the FN1 receptor shift from 5{beta}1 toward CD44 was partly present, whereas the rise of FN1 outside superficial chondrocytes, of FGF1 and of developmental and ossification programs came with progression. Chromatin accessibility changed in the same direction across clusters, with regions linked to FN1 opening and regions linked to ITGA5 closing. OA progression in human cartilage therefore appears to be a change of chondrocyte state that differs in emphasis along a zonal and hypertrophic continuum and includes changes in fibronectin regulation, production, processing, and receptor engagement.

papers.title: Unsupervised prioritization of gene-regulatory variants with isolation forests
papers.abstract: Most common variants occur in non-coding genomic regions. Numerous expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) can influence nearby gene expression. Across diverse traits and diseases, many genome-wide association study (GWAS) loci have been shown to colocalize with eQTLs, supporting gene-regulatory causal mechanisms. However, linkage disequilibrium (LD) obscures the identification of the causal variant(s), necessitating prioritization by functional annotations. Previously published variant prioritization tools relied on the machine-learning-based combination of diverse feature types like evolutionary conservation and chromatin information, whereas more recent deep learning tools learn and describe gene-regulatory DNA sequence grammar. However, the latter approaches often generate a large number of scores per variant. We designed a novel unsupervised machine-learning approach based on isolation forests to integrate the predictions from the broadly used Enformer deep learning model into a single gene-regulatory predictive score for each common variant. Our novel approach eQTL prediction with isolation forests (eQIF) demonstrates strong performance in predicting eQTLs and gene-regulatory GWAS variants. We show that top eQIF variants are located in evolutionarily conserved transcription factor binding site (TFBS) footprints, and that the frequency of top eQIF variants within overrepresented TFBS motifs recapitulates the motif information content. eQIF predictions are precomputed for 9,431,969 common variants and publicly available.

papers.title: scSTEC: Annotating Chromatin Subcompartments from Individual Single-Cell Hi-C Data via Direct Two-Dimensional Embedding and Chromosome-wise Consensus
papers.abstract: textbf{Motivation: }Single-cell Hi-C (scHi-C) technologies enable the study of three-dimensional (3D) genome organization at individual-cell resolution. Many computational methods have been developed to infer hierarchical structures from scHi-C data. However, annotating chromatin subcompartments from sparse scHi-C data remains a challenge. The recently developed scGHOST provides a framework for single-cell subcompartment annotation, but relies on a deep learning-based architecture, a multi-step upstream pipeline involving cell embedding and matrix imputation, and cross-cell information sharing. These features complicate algorithmic interpretation and make the annotation of an individual cell dependent on information from other cells in the dataset. Hence, methods are needed that annotate subcompartments directly from an individual cell's own contact matrix, without complex upstream processing or cross-cell information sharing. textbf{Results: }We developed scSTEC, a computational framework that annotates subcompartments directly from an individual scHi-C matrix without data imputation, complex upstream processing, or cross-cell data sharing. We show that the estimated inter-chromosomal matrix constructed by scGHOST is intrinsically of rank 2, revealing that the geometry relevant to clustering can be represented in two dimensions. Leveraging this low-dimensional structure, scSTEC performs direct subcompartment annotation through 2D genomic embedding and chromosome-wise consensus. Across bulk Hi-C, downsampled simulations, and real scHi-C datasets (four human cell lines, adult mouse cortex, developing mouse embryos, and developing olfactory sensory neurons), scSTEC achieves subcompartment annotations comparable to scGHOST despite operating on each cell independently, while providing greater algorithmic interpretability. Furthermore, subcompartments identified by scSTEC effectively resolve cell types, capture developmental dynamics, and show consistent associations with gene expression and epigenetic profiles. \textbf{Availability: }scSTEC is freely available at url{https://github.com/Ge-lab-pku/scSTEC}.

papers.title: PhenoMe: An interactive AI framework for interpretable, microscopy-driven phenotyping
papers.abstract: Extracting meaningful biological patterns from microscopy image datasets requires tools that quantitatively connect visual similarities and experimental context. Deep learning models, and in particular novel foundation models, have the capacity to translate images into high-dimensional embeddings that can better represent complex visual patterns. Using these complex representations analytically and linking them to experimental information, it is possible to build advanced exploratory and phenotyping capabilities. Here, we present PhenoMe, an open-source, model-agnostic framework to handle pretrained foundation model-derived image representations alongside quantitative image properties and experimental metadata. PhenoMe integrates multiple scriptable and interactive workflows for embedding space visualisation, dimensionality reduction and clustering, similarity-based comparison and retrieval of representative images for each phenotype, among others. It also supports correlation analyses that link the embedding structure to interpretable image properties. We demonstrate PhenoMe's capabilities on seven public microscopy datasets, ranging from cell painting assays, nanoscale synaptic images, drug-response analyses and dynamic cell-phenotyping. These case studies show how readily available image representations can support data contextualisation, curation and analysis. Through guided notebooks, reproducible configurations, extensible model wrappers and a napari plugin, PhenoMe makes representation-based microscopy exploration accessible to researchers without dedicated technical expertise. PhenoMe lays the groundwork for applying foundation models and representation learning to microscopy data analysis.

papers.title: AI-based structural modelling and pathogenic variant mapping across the human protein interactome
papers.abstract: Spanning the complex landscape of the human proteome, physical interactions between proteins coordinate cellular organization, signaling, regulation, and homeostasis. Yet the three-dimensional structures of most of these interactions remain unresolved. Here, we performed AI-based modelling of 109,282 human protein interaction structures, generating a structural resource for large-scale analysis. The predicted structures were systematically characterized through analysis of interface residue involvement, buried surface area, intermolecular bonding, and energetic properties. Additionally, we mapped pathogenic variant data onto the predicted structures, identifying interface-localized mutations for over 4,000 annotated disease categories. Acute myeloid leukemia, Alzheimer's disease, and cardiomyopathy were examined as representative disease contexts for exploring the distribution of interface mutations within disease-associated protein interaction networks. Strengths and limitations of predictive capabilities were also assessed, including through experimental structure comparisons. Collectively, this structural resource and accompanying analyses offer a basis for developing novel hypotheses and informing experimental studies involving human protein interactions in physiological and disease contexts.

papers.title: ARCADE disentangles cell abundance from continuous transcriptional state in spatial transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics is widely used to infer both cell-type abundance and within-type transcriptional variation, but these signals are difficult to separate in mixed spot-level measurements. Here, we present ARCADE, a computational framework that addresses two major sources of uncertainty in spatial analysis: unstable single-cell references and entanglement between abundance and cell state. ARCADE first builds a robust reference through hyperparameter optimization and consensus filtering, then performs spatial inference in two stages by estimating cell-type composition before modeling continuous intratype transcriptional programs around this compositional anchor. Across simulated and semi-synthetic benchmarks, ARCADE improves deconvolution accuracy and yields more stable state inference than existing approaches. In matched human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex datasets with spatial proteogenomic readouts, ARCADE distinguishes localized cell enrichment from astrocyte and microglial activation programs. These results show that decoupled modeling can improve the interpretability of spatial transcriptomic signals in complex tissues.

papers.title: Protein Pocket Coengagement Prioritizes Drug-Drug Interactions
papers.abstract: Drug-drug interactions (DDIs) are largely catalogued empirically, with limited structural explanation of why two drugs interact. We asked whether a purely structural mechanism - competing or cooperating engagement of the same protein pocket - is sufficient to recover documented DDIs without any training on clinical interaction labels. Using composite protein multiple-ligand (COLIG) assignments, which classify co-bound ligand pairs as attractive or repulsive, we scored 21,945 pairs of 210 drugs by predicted engagement of each proteins top-ranked pocket. Confidence-summed COLIG ranking achieved top-5% precision of 49.3% against DDInter and 25.1% against KEGG, versus background prevalences of 29.6% and 14.7%, respectively; pooled top-pocket engagement reached 50.3% DDInter precision. These results support pocket-based DDI screening and class-dependent hypotheses about direct and noncontact ligand engagement, while leaving causal mechanisms to be established.

papers.title: LabWeaver: reliable agentic data analysis grounded in laboratory knowled
papers.abstract: Agentic systems powered by large language models are rapidly automating biological data analysis. However, their reliability remains questionable because they often overlook experimental context, such as disease domain and experimental protocol. Existing agentic systems organize context around individual users and projects, whereas research is organized around laboratories whose projects share experimental context. As a result, experimental context learned in one project remains unavailable to related projects. We introduce LabWeaver, an agentic data analysis framework with a laboratory-organized architecture of three tiers: laboratory, user and project. Further, LabWeaver distills experimental context into laboratory memory and skills, which are shared across users and projects after human-gated review. To isolate the contribution of experimental context, we analyzed a synovial sarcoma single-cell RNA-seq dataset in two sessions that differed only in whether laboratory memory and skills were available. The context-free session lost the fusion reporter at read alignment and misannotated the tumor cells. In contrast, the context-enabled session recovered reporter expression and resolved five fusion-anchored tumor cell states.

papers.title: Follow-up availability and the robustness of immune transcriptomic recovery after myocardial infarction
papers.abstract: Background: Longitudinal blood transcriptomes describe immune changes after myocardial infarction, but later assays do not necessarily represent the population sampled at admission. We examined whether recovery summaries depend on observable selection and assumptions about unavailable assays. Methods: We reanalyzed official processed data from GSE59867, linking 111 patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction across admission, discharge, one month, and six months. Seven fixed Hallmark programs were scored on a common 17,590-gene vocabulary using a bounded within-sample rank statistic. The primary endpoint was the six-month inflammatory-response score. We separated paired-completer change from the observed follow-up mean minus the entire baseline mean; fitted cross-fitted availability and outcome models; and evaluated full-support completion bounds and prespecified missing-mean scenarios. Artificial deletion tested estimators in the 83 observed six-month participants. GSE123342 provided unlinked marginal comparisons and explicitly conditional completion scenarios. Results: GSE59867 contained 101, 95, and 83 follow-up assays. At six months, inflammatory-response change was -0.00893 among paired completers and -0.00999 for the marginal contrast (95% participant-bootstrap interval -0.01217 to -0.00783). Augmented inverse-probability weighting gave -0.01004 (-0.01556 to -0.00727). The full-support completion interval was [-0.16460,0.08765], but eliminating the negative change required an unavailable-assay mean 4.42 observed-follow-up standard deviations above the observed mean. The primary direction remained negative throughout the prespecified {+/-}2-SD scenarios; interferon and coagulation directions were less stable. Under artificial outcome-dependent deletion, all evaluated estimators retained bias. The unlinked external cohort had 65 admission, 64 day-30, and 37 year-one MI assays; the year-one inflammatory contrast was -0.00459, with a conditional tipping shift of 1.70 SD. Conclusions: The observed inflammatory-response rank-score decline was stable to baseline-score adjustment and the prespecified {+/-}2-observed-SD missing-mean scenarios, while unrestricted completion did not identify its direction. Robustness varied across programs and data settings. These findings concern relative transcriptomic scores and assay availability, not clinical recovery, survival, or intervention efficacy.

papers.title: ssGSEA3.0: Feature-Level Bootstrap Resampling for Robust Assessment of Statistical Significance
papers.abstract: Motivation Single-sample Gene/Post-Translational Modification Set Enrichment Analysis (ssGSEA/PTM-SEA) methods assess pathway or signature activity per sample using permutation-based significance testing. ssGSEA2.0's weighted scoring (ssGSEA2.0-orig) uses a correlation-vector reordering that inflates false positives at nonzero weight; directly fixing this (ssGSEA2.0-fixed) restores null-distribution calibration but sacrifices detection power at nonzero weight. Results ssGSEA3.0 replaces feature-label (gene- or site-level) permutation with feature-level bootstrap resampling, which remains calibrated across weighting schemes. On published lung adenocarcinoma and phosphoproteomic perturbation datasets, ssGSEA3.0 shows greater detection power than ssGSEA2.0-fixed, with an additional gain for directional (PTM-SEA) scoring. Previously published findings remain robust across methods, including at nonzero weight. Bootstrapping adds a ~1.5- to 2-fold computational cost. Availability and Implementation ssGSEA3.0 is implemented as an open-source R package (github.com/broadinstitute/ssGSEA3.0, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23734262) and includes the worked examples on biological data presented here.

papers.title: Improving real-time search through deep learning-enhanced fragment ion indexing
papers.abstract: The fragment ion indexed database searching approach enables highly efficient tandem mass spectrometry database searches, including real-time search workflows. However, the index can require tens of gigabytes of memory, often exceeding the free memory available on instrument acquisition computers running the search. This restricts the size of the searchable database, the variable modification space, and the number of searches that can run concurrently. To address this problem, we developed an index-pruning pipeline within the Comet database search tool using Carafe, a deep learning tool that predicts fragment ion intensities based on peptide sequences. In our approach, only fragment ion positions that are predicted to be observable are written in the index, eliminating entries that are unlikely to contribute to spectrum detection. We evaluated this approach on two search spaces in three index configurations to demonstrate that masking significantly reduced the number of fragment ion index entries and, consequently, peak search memory use. Masked searches were also faster than unmasked searches and identified a comparable number of peptide-spectrum matches. Because all prediction and masking steps are performed before searching, their cost is amortized across repeated, future searches of the same database and modification configuration, introducing no per-spectrum search overhead. The complete implementation is open source with an Apache license.

papers.title: VIGAT: VLM-guided gene activity quantification from single-cell ATAC-seq
papers.abstract: Summary: Gene activity quantification from single-cell ATAC-seq is challenging because genomic regions informative of cell identity can vary across genes and tissues, while broadly accessible regions may provide limited cell-type-discriminative information. We developed VIGAT, a vision-language model (VLM)-guided tool that automates visual interpretation of ATAC coverage plots for adaptive gene activity quantification. VIGAT jointly examines accessibility patterns across multiple marker genes, integrating genomic annotations and biological context to select gene-specific regions enriched for cluster-discriminative signals. Selected regions are used to generate a gene-by-cell activity matrix. Across 196 paired single-cell RNA-seq and ATAC-seq datasets, VIGAT outperformed five existing methods in recovering marker-associated accessibility enriched in the corresponding cell populations, demonstrating the utility of VLM-guided visual reasoning for scalable gene activity quantification. Availability and implementation: VIGAT is implemented as an open-source R package and is freely available at https://github.com/beijie02/VIGAT.

papers.title: Bridging Bibliometrics and Biology: A Framework for the Relevance Scoring and Biological Stratification of Scalable MeSH Co-occurrence Networks
papers.abstract: Systematic literature review is often limited by the rigidity of search strings, which often miss non-obvious but highly relevant topics. Controlled vocabularies such as Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) facilitate the review process, but relationships between terms, and their relevance to a hypothesis of interest, are rarely stated explicitly. Presented here is a MeSH term extraction and networking technique, seeded by a single query for Allergic Contact Dermatitis, forming a "themed" network of terms. The resulting co-occurrence network is pruned by an unsupervised consensus of Metropolis-criterion likelihood search strategies, isolating a significant core subgraph and filtering out incidental co-indexing. Symmetrically normalized Article Relevancy Scores (ARS) then evaluate each article against the network's weighted terms across the annotated MEDLINE corpus, correcting for publication volume bias; Mean Relevancy Scoring (MRS) inverts these scores back onto the terms, scoring each MeSH term by the mean ARS of the articles carrying it to measure its specificity to the query. Benchmarked against the expert-curated Adverse Outcome Pathway (AOP) for Allergic Contact Dermatitis, the network recovered key event terminology and identified highly specific literature that standard retrieval methods overlooked. This data-driven approach quantitatively assesses associated MeSH terminology, extracting biologically relevant concepts and key relationships directly from the underlying structure of the literature. By automating the discovery of these latent connections, the framework provides a reproducible, scalable foundation for understanding the biomedical literary space surrounding a given search string, assisting systematic review creation, mechanistic pathway mapping, and hypothesis generation across biomedical disciplines.

papers.title: FastaGuard: FASTA preflight QC for modern bioinformatics pipelines
papers.abstract: Summary: FastaGuard is a streaming, explainable FASTA preflight QC tool that validates assembly FASTA files, detects structural and composition red flags, and emits a versioned multi-format report with an explicit pipeline gate before expensive downstream analysis. We evaluated v1.1.0 in four analyses whose design was fixed before data collection. On 700 public NCBI assemblies the pipeline gate stopped 19.7% (1.9% weighted to the population), always on its high-N rule and mostly in scaffold-level genomes; the NCBI submission gate stopped 2.0%, and an independent recount confirmed every stop. Among 1,040 faults injected into real assemblies, the NCBI gate flagged 520 of 520 in 13 error classes (table2asn: 280 at error level) and blocked none of 120 benign changes. Across seven downstream tools, 46 of 182 defect cells failed and 12 altered the records without a warning, all in classes the pipeline gate blocks. Stopping a mismatched reference at the gate avoided about 54-62 s of mapping and sorting at a cost of 0.05-0.06 s. Availability and Implementation: Source code and documentation are freely available under the MIT license at https://github.com/ehsanestaji/FastaGuard (release tag v1.1.0: https://github.com/ehsanestaji/FastaGuard/releases/tag/v1.1.0; archived at doi:10.5281/zenodo.23728753). Install via Bioconda (mamba install -c conda-forge -c bioconda fastaguard=1.1.0), BioContainers, or GitHub release binaries. Implemented in Rust; supported on Linux and macOS, including Bioconda builds for linux-64, linux-aarch64, osx-64, and osx-arm64. Contact: ehsan.estaji@umu.se; jianfeng.mao@umu.se Supplementary information: Supplementary Note (designs, all results, deviations from the pre-registered protocol); scripts, manifests and result tables at Zenodo, doi:10.5281/zenodo.23729530.

papers.title: DEEPNET-LLM: Highly accurate structure prediction of unknown metabolites from mass spectra via their molecular neighborhoods
papers.abstract: Most molecular features detected by untargeted mass spectrometry-based metabolomics remain unannotated. This so-called 'dark matter' currently comprises more than 90% and likely holds uncharacterized bioactive chemistry. Structure prediction from fragmentation spectra remains an outstanding challenge, because a spectrum does not uniquely determine a structure and the space of candidate structures is mostly unbounded; correspondingly, existing methods rarely return the correct de novo structure as their top prediction. Here we describe De novo Ego network-Enabled Propagation and Neighborhood Extrapolation of Topology using Large Language Models (DEEPNET-LLM) reasoning approach, which uses Molecular Community Networking (MCN) to restrict the search of a query spectrum to its local neighborhood within the global metabolome, and applies AI reasoning to propagate structural information from neighbors to the query. For a collection of 900 authentic standards (2,249 spectra) that have never been publicly released to exclude possibility of data leakage, DEEPNET-LLM returned the correct structure as its top prediction for 84.7% of spectra. Accuracy was independent of precursor mass across a range over which the number of candidate structures grows by 30 orders of magnitude, and was comparable across ion polarity, adducts and in-source fragmentation. On a random subset of the public MassSpecGym benchmark, DEEPNET-LLM reached 85.9% top-1 accuracy excluding stereochemistry. We showcase the use of DEEPNET-LLM with an example of a discovery of tryptamine amidate of a bile acid in mouse gut, confirmed against a synthetic standard. The DEEPNET-LLM approach is orthogonal to existing in silico methods and can be combined with them.

papers.title: A comparison of two culture and three sequencing methods for detection of the urobiome
papers.abstract: Standard urine culture (SUC), the clinical reference method, is optimized for fast-growing aerobes and misses much of the urinary microbiota. Enhanced culture and sequencing methods have rarely been compared on the same specimens. We compared five methods (SUC, expanded quantitative urine culture [EQUC], short-read V4 16S rRNA gene sequencing, long-read near full-length 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and PCR-free long-read shotgun metagenomic sequencing) on parallel aliquots of urine from pregnant participants screened for asymptomatic bacteriuria. Of 98 cultured samples, 98 (100.0%) were EQUC-positive while 85 (86.7%) SUC-positive. EQUC detected 102 species, but SUC only detected 41. Short-read 16S rRNA gene sequencing, long-read 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and shotgun sequencing were positive for 188/188, 186/188 and 139/139 samples, detecting 195, 69 and 528 species, respectively. In the 79 samples positive by EQUC and all three sequencing methods, sequencing profiles resembled each other more than culture profiles, and SUC captured only a subset of taxa detected by every other method. Shotgun sequencing gave the broadest taxonomic coverage and was the only sequencing method to identify Escherichia coli to the species level. With EQUC, it outperformed both 16S sequencing methods in detecting Gardnerella vaginalis and distinguishing Lactobacillus species, and it resolved six Gardnerella species, three detected by no other method. Long-read 16S rRNA gene sequencing gave the most confident amplicon-based species assignments, whereas culture better recovered Corynebacterium and Staphylococcus species. No single method was best across all endpoints, but long-read shotgun metagenomics provided the broadest species-level view. Method choice should match the research or clinical question; outcome-based studies are needed to establish clinical utility.

papers.title: BioResearchBench: 50 Long Horizon Biological Research Tasks
papers.abstract: AI models are used in biology research to study disease mechanisms, discover potential treatments, analyze experimental data, troubleshoot problems, and plan next steps. Useful assistance depends on working with data in various scientific formats, interpreting results, and deciding what to test next. We present BioResearchBench, a benchmark of 50 research questions developed by PhD biologists drawing on their deep research expertise to reflect realistic problems encountered in their fields. Questions were refined through expert review and iterative model testing. The collection spans 10 diverse biology subdomains and includes sequencing data, proteomic measurements, microscopy images, assay readouts, and clinical datasets. We compared recorded outcomes and examined model responses in depth across the 50 tasks on OpenAI GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 4 Argon, Meta Muse Wonder, and SpaceXSI Grok 4.7. Success across our benchmark was 18% for Claude Opus 5.5, 13% for Gemini 4 Argon, 11% for Meta Muse Wonder, 4% for GPT-6 Astra, and 4% for Grok 4.7. These results describe a deliberately challenging collection selected through expert review and model testing. Despite low whole task success, the selected responses met most rubric requirements on average: the average fraction of criteria missed ranged from 18% to 32% across models. Across models, the proportion of eligible tasks with at least one category failure was highest in computation and data handling (66.9% failure), followed by uncertainty and identification (55.3% failure), reporting and completeness (54.7% failure), biological interpretation (39.0% failure), controls and causal claims (37.2% failure), and choosing the next experiment or decision (31.0% failure). Gemini 4 Argon had the highest proportion of reviewed tasks without a recorded category failure in computation and data handling (45% success) and biological interpretation (69% success). Claude Opus 5.5 led in controls and causal claims (72% success) and choosing the next experiment or decision (75% success). GPT-6 Astra led in uncertainty and identification (56% success) which included judging the precision of estimates and recognizing when measurements could not distinguish between biological explanations. GPT-6 Astra and Meta Muse Wonder tied for the highest proportion of answers with no recorded omissions or reporting failures (51% success). Five case studies presented here show how top AI models can perform many analytical steps correctly yet misinterpret what results signify. For example, some answers described cells as fully recovered when oxygen consumption improved even though mitochondrial membrane potential and cell number remained below control levels. These model answers therefore overstated the extent of cell recovery. Other answers incorrectly called a protein a direct microRNA target, although the experiment had not tested whether the microRNA acted directly on its mRNA or affected it through another process. In a protein turnover task, some model answers misestimated protein half-lives because they did not account for the gradual labeling of amino acids used to make new proteins. These model errors can lead researchers to pursue the wrong explanation even when individual analytical steps are completed correctly. This matters for major scientific goals such as drug discovery, where progress depends on choosing useful experiments and tools, interpreting unexpected results, troubleshooting failed approaches, and deciding which direction is most worth pursuing. Evaluating AI research assistance therefore requires checking whether its explanations, conclusions, and proposed experiments follow from the data and experimental design. These cases highlight continuing challenges in scientific reasoning for frontier AI models: bringing together different types of biological data, analyzing them with appropriate tools and databases, and using the results to draw appropriate conclusions and guide the next steps in research. The observed errors suggest training priorities in data analysis, biological interpretation, and experimental judgment and motivate evaluations that follow researchers and models through iterative scientific work.

papers.title: CNVision: a computational framework for functional interpretation of intragenic copy number variants
papers.abstract: Background Intragenic copy number variants (CNVs), including exon-level deletions and duplications within a single gene, represent an important class of pathogenic genomic variation. Their functional consequences depend on the precise relationship between the CNV breakpoints, exon structure, coding sequence boundaries, transcript orientation, and reading frame. Although intragenic CNVs contribute substantially to Mendelian disease, their interpretation remains difficult because many existing workflows rely on manual transcript review or annotation pipelines that do not consistently resolve exon-level and base-pair-level consequences. Results We developed CNVision, a containerized computational framework for standardized interpretation of intragenic CNVs. CNVision accepts multiple input formats, including exon-based entries, genomic coordinates, and HGVS genomic notation, and converts each into a unified internal representation for transcript-aware analysis. The system maps CNVs to coding sequence regions, calculates affected coding sequence length at base-pair resolution, and classifies predicted reading-frame consequence. CNVision was evaluated using a dataset including 200 curated intragenic CNVs spanning multiple genes, genome builds, variant structures, and input types. Across the dataset, CNVision produced predictions concordant with manual transcript-level analysis and correctly processed exon-based, coordinate-based, and HGVS-formatted inputs. Beyond basic evaluation, CNVision also identified discrepancies in previously published CNVs. Of 131 reported CNVs evaluated, 15 yielded classifications that differed from the original published interpretation; independent manual transcript-level analysis using the UCSC Genome Browser supported CNVision's classification in all 15 variants, indicating the discrepancies were attributable to differences in transcript interpretation or coordinate calculation rather than computational error. In terms of processing speed, CNVision was tested by two board-certified laboratory geneticists who compared the runtime of CNVision versus manual analysis across 18 CNVs, 6 of each input type. CNVision consistently outperformed manual analysis by both geneticists across all variants by a significant margin. Conclusion CNVision provides a reproducible framework for functional interpretation of intragenic CNVs by automating input parsing, transcript mapping, coding sequence overlap calculation, and reading-frame classification. The framework reduces manual burden, improves consistency, and provides a foundation for future expansion into batch CNV processing and graphical variant interpretation.

papers.title: Ark-ADMET: endpoint-specific selection of molecular representations and hyperparameters for gradient-boosted ADMET models under the Therapeutics Data Commons benchmark protocol
papers.abstract: Typical submissions to the Therapeutics Data Commons (TDC) absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity (ADMET) benchmark leaderboard apply a single architecture and a single feature representation across all 22 endpoints, despite substantial heterogeneity in evaluation metric, training-set size, and class balance. Rather than proposing a new architecture, we show that endpoint-specific selection of molecular representations and CatBoost hyperparameters, carried out under the official TDC ADMET benchmark protocol, is a competitive alternative to that uniform recipe. For each endpoint, a fixed CatBoost backbone was paired with configurations chosen from a common candidate set comprising published fingerprints and physicochemical descriptors, truncated three-dimensional PaDEL descriptors, frozen graph isomorphism network (GIN) and MiniMol embeddings, and a convex combination with a shallow network trained on the MiniMol embedding alone. All feature and hyperparameter choices were made on an internal scaffold validation split under a prespecified strict-improvement rule. Against a frozen snapshot of the public leaderboard, the resulting Ark-ADMET family of 22 endpoint-specific models matched or exceeded the best previously listed score on 7 of 21 rankable endpoints and strictly exceeded it on 3. All selected configurations retain the baseline fingerprint-and-descriptor block; optional components differ across endpoints. Taken together, these results show that competitive performance on this benchmark can be achieved without a new architecture or a single optional representation shared across all endpoints.

papers.title: Phylogeny-Guided Global-Local Shrinkage for Microbiome Feature Selection
papers.abstract: Microbiome feature selection is challenging because sequencing counts are sparseand compositional, while evolutionarily related taxa may exhibit similar associations with an exposure. We propose phylogeny-guided global--local shrinkage (PGL), a Bayesian regression method for identifying exposure-associated differences in the relative abundances of individual amplicon sequence variants (ASVs). A multinomial logit-normal working model analyzes relative abundance among ASVs detected in each sample. A zero-sum constraint gives the regression coefficients a log-ratio interpretation relative to the mean across retained ASVs. Global--local shrinkage accommodates weak and large associations, while an estimated weight controls information sharing along a supplied phylogenetic tree. Simulation ablation studies showed that phylogenetic borrowing improved detection power and estimation of nonzero coefficients when associations aligned with the tree, with little change under a tree-independent generator. Estimated borrowing decreased as the supplied tree was corrupted. Comparisons with benchmark methods revealed different trade-offs between detection power and false discovery rates across simulation settings. In an HIV oral microbiome application, ablation analysis showed that phylogenetic borrowing preserved the overall pattern of estimated associations while changing posterior uncertainty and selecting three additional ASVs. PGL provides ASV-level inference with adaptive information sharing across evolutionarily related features.

papers.title: LOTUS: lineage-aware optimal transport reconstructs continuous clonal fate dynamics
papers.abstract: Destructive sampling in single-cell sequencing obscures ancestor-descendant relationships, limiting the continuous reconstruction of cell-fate dynamics. Here we present Lineage-aware optimal transport for unbalanced single-cell dynamics (LOTUS), a framework that integrates time-resolved transcriptomic snapshots with clonal lineage information from engineered barcodes or endogenous T cell receptor clonotypes. LOTUS couples clone-level optimal transport with neural unbalanced transport to model continuous cellular state change, population growth and clonal propagation under lineage-consistent constraints. In branching simulations, LOTUS reduced lineage-inconsistent transport relative to benchmark methods, lowering off-target routing from 4.94-14.84% to 1.10%. On LARRY lineage-barcode scRNA-seq of hematopoiesis, LOTUS reconstructed branching trajectories, improved early neutrophil-monocyte fate-boundary prediction, and inferred multi-fate progenitors and fate-biased meta-clones, linking their distinct fate potentials to inferred epigenetic priming. On CellTagging scRNA-seq of fibroblast reprogramming, it distinguished reprogrammed from failed trajectories and prioritized fate-associated perturbation genes. In longitudinal scRNA-seq and TCR-seq of malaria-responsive memory (CD45RA-) CD4+ T cells, it preserved endogenous clonotype structure and reconstructed TR1 dynamics and regulatory networks. LOTUS thus converts lineage-resolved single-cell snapshots into interpretable, continuous models of fate dynamics and their regulatory programs.

papers.title: A validation approach for RNA structures based on deep-learning 3D-structure predictions
papers.abstract: Understanding the molecular mechanisms of life depends on accurate macromolecular structures. RNA, in particular, poses a particular challenge for structural biology due to its inherent flexibility and dynamic nature. The challenging nature of structure determination experiments and their interpretation have led to the development of validation approaches to prevent or fix errors in solved structures. Existing methods for RNA structure validation can, as with proteins, be broadly split into two types. Map-based validation tools seek to detect discrepancies between the experimental data and the determined structure. They are excellent for fixing all types of errors, but only when high-resolution experimental data are available.Model-only validation methods, which usually focus on molecular geometry, are excellent for fixing short-length-scale issues even when experimental resolution is low. Conkit-validate is a mapless method for protein validation, which is not based on chemical plausibility, but rather on the similarity between experimental models and structure predictions for the same protein. By comparing contact patterns, this tool leverages evolutionary covariance information, learned by state-of-the-art structural prediction models, into a mapless validation method capable of detecting sequence assignment issues, with notable success in detecting register errors. Here, we extend the conkit-validate method to work on RNA.The results show performance similar to that previously achieved for proteins. %We also show how this new method can detect errors missed by map-based approaches when the experimental data is of low resolution. In a scan of the PDB, its detection rate does not depend on the local resolution of the density, so it remains applicable where map-based approaches are not, and case studies show it can identify register errors where the density alone cannot decide between models.Together, this highlights the complementary value of a contact-prediction based validation approach using information orthogonal to map- and geometry-based approaches to ensure the quality of deposited RNA structures against varying criteria.The performance of the method can be expected to track ongoing improvements in RNA structure prediction methods.

papers.title: irAEGIS: Pathway-guided interpretable prediction of immune-related adverse events
papers.abstract: Immune-related adverse events (irAEs) are major complications of immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy and remain difficult to predict prior to treatment initiation. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) provides a unique opportunity to characterize immune states associated with future irAE development. However, translating single-cell measurements into accurate and biologically interpretable patient-level risk predictions remains challenging. Existing approaches typically aggregate cellular profiles into patient-level summaries, thereby obscuring cell type specific signals, or rely on complex deep-learning architectures that offer limited insight into the biological pathways and mechanisms underlying their predictions. Here, we present irAEGIS, a pathway-guided interpretable model for predicting irAE risk from pre-treatment scRNA-seq data. irAEGIS incorporates prior biological knowledge through gene set constrained representation learning, aggregates pathway activities within individual cell types, and integrates cell type specific risk signals through a hierarchical prediction framework. This design enables predictions to be decomposed into contributions from individual cell types, pathways, and genes, providing interpretable explanations across multiple biological resolutions. Across simulated datasets and independent pre-treatment ICI cohorts, irAEGIS consistently outperformed seven existing methods. Beyond predictive performance, irAEGIS identified biologically coherent immune programs associated with irAE risk. In non-small cell lung cancer, irAEGIS highlighted neutrophil-associated inflammatory pathways linked to future irAE development, whereas in melanoma, it identified apoptotic and immune activation pathways in CD8+ NKT-like cells associated with severe irAEs. These findings were independently supported by pathway enrichment, cell-cell communication, and trajectory analyses. Together, irAEGIS provides a biologically informed and interpretable model for linking single-cell immune states to patient outcomes, enabling both accurate risk prediction and mechanistic insight into immune-related adverse events. More broadly, irAEGIS establishes a general strategy for interpretable phenotype prediction and biological discovery from single-cell transcriptomic data.

papers.title: Aging reshapes cardiac extravascular leukocyte transcription through bidirectional remodeling during LPS-induced endotoxemia
papers.abstract: Sepsis disproportionately affects older adults and is frequently complicated by cardiac dysfunction. However, how aging alters the transcriptional responses of cardiac extravascular immune cells during systemic inflammation remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated aging-dependent transcriptional remodeling of cardiac immune cells using an LPS-induced endotoxemia model in young and aged C57BL/6 mice. Mice received intraperitoneal LPS (5 mg/kg body weight) or vehicle, and cardiac extravascular leukocytes were isolated from ex vivo retrogradely perfused hearts 24 h later for single-cell RNA sequencing. Aging was associated with bidirectional transcriptional remodeling, characterized by both up- and downregulation of gene programs, particularly in cardiac macrophages, monocyte-like macrophages, T cells, and B cells following LPS challenge. A shared feature across these four cell populations was reduced representation of mitochondrial-associated transcriptional programs, indicating aging-dependent remodeling of mitochondrial biology across cardiac myeloid and lymphoid lineages during systemic inflammation. In parallel, cell type-specific transcriptional remodeling revealed distinct functional-associated responses. Macrophages and monocyte-like macrophages exhibited increased tissue-remodeling and repair-associated transcriptional programs. Both T and B cells showed reduced metabolic programs but increased actin cytoskeleton organization. T cells additionally exhibited reduced cytotoxicity-associated and enhanced Th17-associated transcriptional programs, whereas B cells showed reduced antigen-processing and presentation programs. Cell-cell communication analysis suggested aging-associated differences in immune cell interactions following LPS challenge and potential features of cardiac inflammaging at baseline. Together, these findings demonstrate that aging bidirectionally reshapes the cardiac immune response to systemic inflammation, characterized by shared remodeling of mitochondrial-associated programs and cell type-specific changes in inflammatory, metabolic, cytoskeletal, and effector-associated programs. These aging-dependent transcriptional changes occurred in the context of the greater severity of illness observed in aged mice following LPS-induced endotoxemia.

papers.title: Continuous Topological Accessibility (RFA) as a 3D-Aware GRN Filter: Anticorrelation with eQTL and No Prediction of ΔRNA
papers.abstract: We formalize Relative Forest Accessibility (RFA), a topological accessibility index computed as the solution of (I - {gamma}P )x = v0, where P is a Markov transition matrix built from Hi-C contacts and v0 is a vector of TF peaks (or ATAC peaks). RFA yields a continuous accessibility profile across all genomic bins. We test RFA on three targets. First, on promoter TF counts (GM12878 chr1, 10 kb, 811 genes), RFA loses to 1D distance (AUC 0.836 vs 0.976); this is an artifact because the target and the 1D distance look at the same window. Second, on eQTL (GTEx v10 LCL, chr1+17+19, 10 kb, 1625 genes), RFA anticorrelates with eQTL: {rho}(RFA, - log10 pmin) = -0.09, AUC(RFA) = 0.386 (below chance), AUC(-RFA) = 0.614. High RFA corresponds to fewer eQTL, and dose-response analysis confirms that AUC(RFA) decreases with eQTL strength (mean trend -0.056, 19/20 TFs). A distance-preserving shuffle of the Hi-C matrix reproduces this anticorrelation ({triangleup}AUC vs real: [-0.074, +0.076] across 5 TFs, all CIs include 0), whereas a degree-preserving rewiring destroys it ({triangleup}AUC [isin] [-0.261, -0.003], CIs exclude 0 for 5/5 TFs); the anticorrelation therefore reflects distance-decay of Hi-C contacts (local 3D accessibility), not higher-order topology. The anticorrelation replicates on chr17 ({triangleup}{rho} = -0.13 for rewired, 0/5 for shuffled) and on chr19 with an inverted control pattern, consistent with local within-diagonal heterogeneity as the carrier on short gene-dense chromosomes. Third, on {triangleup}RNA (MCF10A vs MCF7, 40 kb, ATAC peaks), RFA does not predict {triangleup}RNA ({rho} = +0.005, permutation p = 0.87, bootstrap 95% CI [-0.040, +0.053], n = 1730); the CI includes zero and does not exclude the practical boundary |{rho}| = 0.05. Within-line sanity checks are also null. We conclude that RFA anticorrelates with eQTL via local distance-decay and does not predict {triangleup}RNA. The anticorrelation is carried by distance-decay, not by loops or TADs, and may reflect expression buffering: genes with strong eQTL are less dependent on local 3D accessibility. RFA is not a universal predictor but a filter with an inverted sign on eQTL and no signal on {triangleup}RNA.
